cases.question: What provisions does the guidance describe for operation and maintenance of rural water supply systems?
retrieved_filenames: AssamDistrict wise number of Rural Population as on (01.xls
cases.answer:
The guidance requires district-level O&M planning for all schemes, covering total O&M cost for rural water supply (energy costs, preventive maintenance, breakdown maintenance, payment for O&M staff, water quality testing, and other O&M charges), the proposed water tariff, whether the tariff covers O&M charges, how any shortfall would be met, and existing O&M funds allocation. [3]

VWSC/Pani Samiti is the village-level Gram Panchayat standing committee constituted to plan, implement, manage and oversee in-village rural piped water supply systems. [7]

JJM-2 guidelines include chapters on commissioning and handing-over protocol for rural piped water supply schemes and on commissioning, handover and annual source maintenance. [8]

I could not find sufficient evidence in the available JJM corpus for a fuller description of O&M operational rules, funding mechanisms, or implementation procedures beyond the planning items and institutional roles above.

cases.question: What responsibilities are assigned to Gram Panchayats or VWSCs in implementing village water supply systems?
retrieved_filenames: CS1 B (ii). Robust chlorination system_ Disinfecti.xls
cases.answer:
Gram Panchayats (GPs) and/or their sub-committees (VWSC/Paani Samiti/User Group, etc.) are assigned a lead community role in planning, implementation, management, operation and maintenance of in-village water supply infrastructure. Gram Sabha decides whether the GP or sub-committee carries out water supply management. [3][7]

The GP and/or sub-committee will discharge the following functions: [3]
- provide FHTC to every existing rural HH and any new HH that may emerge in future, and ensure that scattered households located away from main settlements also get FHTCs
- ensure preparation of Village Action Plan (VAP) for water supply scheme
- plan, design, implement, operate and maintain the in-village water supply schemes and decide seasonal supply hours
- procure construction services/goods/materials from agencies/vendors as finalized by SWSM through centralized item rate tendering
- mobilize and motivate the community to contribute 5% or 10% of in-village infrastructure capital expenditure (in cash and/or kind and/or labour)
- supervise construction of in-village infrastructure including source sustainability, greywater reuse, water conservation measures, etc.
- open bank account/use existing account of GP for community contribution and depositing O&M service charge (with a separate ledger if an existing account is used)
- create and maintain register for accounts reflecting community contribution, construction costs, O&M costs/water tariff collection and incentive received
- mobilize community for PRA activities
- firm up and collect water tariff/user charges
- be responsible for management and regular O&M of in-village water supply system including local water sources
- record drinking water asset details in GP/village asset register
- facilitate trial runs on scheme completion
- facilitate third party inspection and functionality assessment
- hold periodic meetings at least four times in a year and maintain minutes/record of the same
- ensure water quality testing using Field Test Kits (FTKs), periodic testing at laboratories and disseminate the same among community and undertake sanitary inspection (engage/train rural youth/students/women)
- may engage a dedicated person to ensure water quality test using FTKs, as per the respective State policy
- undertake social audit

For stand-alone systems in scattered settlements/habitations, a user group is formed to own, manage, operate and maintain the system and is accountable to the GP and/or its sub-committee. [3]

GP and/or its sub-committee will function as a legal entity as envisaged in the 73rd Amendment to the Constitution. Community willingness (via Gram Sabha resolution and contribution) is the foremost criterion for planning. [7]

cases.question: What quantity and quality of drinking water does the JJM FHTC guidance describe?
cases.answer:
**Quantity: at least 55 lpcd (adequate quantity); quality: BIS:10500 / IS 10500:2012 prescribed standard (as amended).**

JJM defines an FHTC as a rural household tap connection providing drinking water in adequate quantity of prescribed quality on a regular basis [7]. Functionality of a tap connection is defined as infrastructure providing water in adequate quantity (at least 55 lpcd) of prescribed quality (BIS:10500 standard) on a regular basis (continuous supply in the long term) [7]. The same quantity and quality targets appear in the strategy section: FHTC delivering water in adequate quantity (minimum 55 lpcd) of prescribed quality (BIS:10500) on a regular basis as decided by the Gram Panchayat and/or its sub-committee [3]. The BIS reference is given as IS 10500:2012 ‘Indian Standard – Drinking Water Specification’ as amended from time to time [7]. Other excerpts refer to potable water in adequate quantity of prescribed quality or water meeting BIS 10500, without adding different numeric or standard values [2][8][10].

cases.question: How does the guidance describe community participation in JJM planning and service delivery?
retrieved_filenames: Format - F27 Status of Pipe Water Supply in Ashram.xls
Format B15 _ Piped water supply schemes.xls
cases.answer:
The guidance describes community participation as central to JJM, with Gram Panchayats and local communities (including VWSC/Paani Samiti/User Group) playing a critical role in planning, implementation, management, operation and maintenance of in-village water supply. Community-led partnership with States/UTs is the strategy, with communities expected to have participation, ownership and contribution in all decisions on water supply systems; States/UTs act as facilitators to support long-term sustainability. The revenue village (with habitations) is the unit for planning, implementation, monitoring, management, O&M. VWSC/Pani Samiti is defined as the village-level standing committee of the Gram Panchayat constituted to plan, implement, manage and oversee in-village rural piped water supply systems. [3][7]

For water quality in service delivery, village-level surveillance is undertaken through community participation via trained Sujalam Shakti Groups (women’s SHGs), using Field Test Kits and digital platforms for routine monitoring, early identification of issues, local ownership and last-mile vigilance. This integrates with laboratory testing to reinforce shared responsibility and Jan Bhagidari, shifting toward continuous, community-led, technology-enabled governance. [2][7]

JJM 2.0 embeds community engagement across the full service delivery lifecycle (planning through O&M, handing over, monitoring and sustainability) via two-way communication and IEC tools such as Jal Arpan (formal handing over of schemes to GP/community), Jal Utsav, Gram Sabha/Jal Chaupal, Jal Seva Aankalan, Pey Jal Samvad and Sujal Gram Samvad. These enable feedback, dialogue, participatory oversight, continuous community learning on O&M roles, and use of community input for planning, course correction and accountability. VWSCs/GPs are to be strengthened as micro-utilities under a utility-based service delivery framework, with participatory mechanisms for citizen engagement and grievance redressal. [5][8]

I could not find sufficient evidence in the available JJM corpus on any quantitative targets or detailed step-by-step procedures for community participation beyond the descriptions above.

cases.question: What does the operational material say about water quality monitoring and surveillance?
cases.answer:
The operational guidelines distinguish drinking water quality monitoring from water quality surveillance. Monitoring is done by the PHED/RWS Department (the supplier/agency responsible for water quality) via laboratory and field testing of samples from sources and FHTCs, using existing State/District/Sub-division/Block laboratories plus mobile laboratories where possible. Surveillance at the grassroots is the responsibility of GPs/rural community. [3]

Water quality testing is described as important for monitoring water-supply operation, verifying drinking-water safety, investigating disease outbreaks, validation, and preventive measures; tools are to be used at the source, within piped distribution, or at the consumer end. [3]

Every Gram Panchayat and/or its sub-committee (VWSC/Paani Samiti/User Group) is to identify and train five women in every village to undertake surveillance. Surveillance activities include use of Field Test Kits (FTKs) at GP level (with positively tested samples referred to a nearby laboratory for confirmation) and sanitary inspection (an on-site investigative activity to identify actual and potential sources of microbiological contamination, evaluate physical structure/operation and external factors such as toilet location, and enable timely remedial action). Sanitary inspections are to be carried out for all new and existing sources from time to time; results and needed remedial actions are to be discussed with the community. In JE-AES and Acute Diarrhoeal Diseases affected districts, sanitary inspection twice a year is advised. [3]

The guidelines note that communities typically judge quality only by colour, odour and taste, so chemical contaminants often go unnoticed; awareness, education and community engagement in surveillance are therefore required. Listed activities include awareness and education programmes on water quality in Schools, Anganwadi centres, Health centres, GPs/PRIs, etc., plus awareness generation and capacity building of stakeholders. [3]

WQM&S is subsumed under JJM and will receive up to 2% of JJM funds (further details in Chapter 10). [7] DWSM is to include a Coordinator for WQM&S (remuneration, if contractual, from the support-activity fund). [10]

Under the later operational guidelines (JJM 2.0), States/UTs are to shift from periodic testing to continuous, technology-enabled, response-based water quality governance, with a year-wise budgeted framework for WQM&S and digital reporting (covering human resources, laboratory operations, consumables, FTKs, digital portable field test kits and community-led mechanisms). Reform aims include a shift from reactive to preventive management with early detection; empowered community-led monitoring via trained Sujalam Shakti Groups; continuous monitoring and data-driven decision-making via digital dashboards; a strengthened laboratory ecosystem; and transparency through public dashboards and accessible information. Village-level surveillance is to be undertaken through community participation by trained women groups designated as Sujalam Shakti (from women’s SHGs under SRLM, trained and certified at NSQF Level-1 in basic testing and surveillance); data are to be captured via prescribed digital platforms including the Sujal Gaon Utility App and integrated into centralised dashboards for real-time visibility, alerts and remedial actions. [4][8]

Support and WQM&S fund utilisation is to be aligned with reforms, prioritising critical gaps in monitoring, surveillance and system strengthening, mapped and tracked on JJM IMIS; indicative areas include digital governance and monitoring systems, institutional strengthening, capacity building, IEC/BCC and community mobilisation, research and innovation, and water quality monitoring and surveillance. Release of Support and WQM&S funds is subject to activity-wise reconciliation, UCs and audited statements. [2]

The supplied spreadsheet extracts contain only numeric rows (state-wise figures) and do not describe operational policy on monitoring or surveillance. [1][5][6][9]

cases.question: What implementation responsibilities are described for States and Union Territories under JJM?

cases.answer:
The supplied evidence describes the following implementation responsibilities for States and Union Territories under JJM (including JJM 2.0 operational material). These are taken from the guideline excerpts; population, habitation, and benchmark tables in the evidence do not describe responsibilities.

**Citizen interface, feedback, and grievance systems [8]**  
Roles and responsibilities of States/UTs include:  
- Enable Citizen Interface: ensure adoption and effective use of the Meri Panchayat Application as the primary citizen interface for accessing information, submitting feedback and tracking grievances.  
- Ensure Data Integration and Availability: ensure integration of Sujalam Bharat DPI, Project Monitoring Module and Sujal Gaon Utility Application with citizen platforms so that accurate and up-to-date information on schemes, service delivery and progress is available.  
- Link Feedback with Service Areas: ensure that all citizen feedback and grievances are linked to Sujal Gaon IDs to enable precise identification of issues and targeted resolution.  
- Establish Grievance Redressal Mechanism: define clear workflows, timelines and escalation mechanisms for addressing citizen feedback across Gram Panchayat, District and State levels.  
- Monitor Feedback and Response: use dashboards to monitor grievance status, resolution timelines and service delivery outcomes and ensure timely action by responsible authorities.  
- Strengthen Accountability: assign clear responsibilities to Districts, VWSCs and service providers for responding to citizen feedback and regularly review performance.  
- Capacity Building and Awareness: undertake awareness campaigns and training to encourage citizens and local institutions to use digital platforms for feedback and participation.

**Water quality monitoring and surveillance (WQM&S) [5]**  
- State/UT must establish year-wise budgeted financial arrangements that enable a sustainable and accountable framework for WQM&S and digital reporting systems that are adequately resourced. This includes planning and securing long-term funds for human resources, laboratory operations, consumables, Field Test Kits (FTKs), digital portable field test kits and community-led monitoring & surveillance mechanisms. Strengthening of institutional capacities, supported by an annually earmarked financial budget, shall ensure sustained operation of continuous monitoring & surveillance systems.  
- Under JJM 2.0, States/UTs shall progressively shift from periodic testing practices to a continuous, technology-enabled monitoring and response-based water quality governance system. Village-level surveillance shall be undertaken through community participation (Sujalam Shakti groups). All WQM&S activities shall be digitised, with data captured through prescribed digital platforms (including the Sujal Gaon Utility App) and integrated for real-time visibility. States may additionally customise Block/Sub-divisional level arrangements (text cuts off).

**Programme fund utilisation, reconciliation, and financial management [2]**  
- States shall undertake detailed reconciliation to verify expenditures against approved and reform-linked activities, identify unspent balances and liabilities, and ensure alignment between financial reporting and physical progress on JJM IMIS. Only validated expenditure shall be considered for subsequent releases.  
- States shall prepare a utilisation plan aligned with Section 2 reforms and CIRP-linked outcomes, prioritising critical gaps in monitoring, surveillance and system strengthening; all proposed activities shall be mapped and tracked on JJM IMIS.  
- Expenditure under Support and WQM&S components shall be linked to achievement of defined milestones, implementation of structural reforms outlined in Section 2, and progress on JJM IMIS.  
- States shall ensure that utilisation of Support funds is mapped to reform-linked activities, is outcome-driven, and is mandatorily reported on JJM IMIS.  
- States shall ensure that funds are utilised in a timely, efficient and outcome-oriented manner in alignment with approved plans and reform priorities. Financial management systems shall enable transparency, accountability and end-to-end traceability of expenditures through PFMS-compliant processes, aligned with data reported on JJM IMIS.

cases.question: What does the policy say about FHTC delivery, and what household connection measure is reported for Khammam?
cases.answer:
**Policy on FHTC delivery (from operational guidelines):** In-village piped water supply infrastructure for SVS schemes consists of source development/augmentation, sustainability measures, treatment (if needed), pumping, OHT/sump and a distribution network leading to FHTC; for MVS schemes it consists of pumping, OHT/sump, pipeline, distribution network leading up to FHTC, and bulk metering. Existing functional piped systems are to be retrofitted to provide FHTCs (distribution network plus augmentation to at least 55 lpcd service level, plus greywater management). Service level of potable supply should be at least 55 lpcd. [4]

For PMAY(G) houses, JJM funds are to be used in convergence; tap connections are to come from the existing village distribution network with no new distribution network created. [8]

- House connections as on 15/08/2019: 107304 [2]  
- House connections as on 23/08/2026: 270254 [9]  
- FHTC coverage (in %): 100.00 [6]  

These come from Progress at district level.xls (column structure in [1]). There is an internal inconsistency in the supplied structured facts: [6] lists 100% FHTC coverage with report_date=15/08/2019, but that date’s house-connection figure [2] is far below total households [5]; the 100% figure aligns with the later “as on 23/08/2026” connections equaling total households [9]. State-level tables show Telangana at 100% FHTC but do not break out Khammam. [3][7][10]
